newsitem.title: GERMANY: Court convicts Stasi officers of aiding guerrillas.
newsitem.headline: Court convicts Stasi officers of aiding guerrillas.

text.p: A Berlin court sentenced three former East German intelligence officers to two years' probation on Friday for helping ten of West Germany's most wanted urban guerrillas escape justice.

Harry Dahl, 67, chief of the counter-terrorism department in the once feared Ministry for State Security (Stasi), and two officers, Guenter Jaeckel, 62, and Gerd Zaumseil, 48, were convicted of preventing the course of justice.

The case was the latest to try to establish how far East Berlin supported international terrorism and punish those behind an "unholy alliance" between the Stasi and the leftist Red Army Faction (RAF), that struck fear into the West German establishment during the 1970s and 1980s.
The court also issued formal reprimands to the three Stasi officers and said they would be fined between 2,400 marks ($1,400) and 5,000 marks ($2,900) if they violated the terms of their probation.
Charges were dropped against a fourth former Stasi officer, Hans-Hermann Petzold, 52, on Wednesday who originally went on trial with them in the middle of last month.

The men were charged with granting the 10 guerrillas entry into communist East Germany, creating identities for them, and giving them flats and jobs to blend them into everyday life there from 1980 to 1990, thus helping them escape authorities in the West.
Some of the guerrillas were regarded as West Germany's most dangerous criminals, although they were regarded as retired after moving to East Germany.

Susanne Albrecht had been wanted for her part in the 1977 murder of banker Juergen Ponto, the chairman of Dresdner Bank in Frankfurt. Silke Maier-Witt and Monika Helbing were wanted in connection with the 1977 kidnapping and murder of Employers' Federation chief Hanns-Martin Schleyer.
The guerrillas were given refuge on orders from former Stasi chief Erich Mielke and witnesses testified that East German head of state Erich Honecker knew of the operation.
The arrests of the ten guerrillas in summer 1990 shocked Germans on both sides of the Cold War divide.

Defence lawyers in the case argued their clients did not dispute they helped give the retired guerrillas a new start in life, but denied the charges, saying their action helped ward off the greater evil of more potential guerrilla attacks.

Normally former East German citizens can only be tried for breaking the laws of the former communist country, but in this case they were tried according to current federal law which punishes prevention of justice with up to five years jail.

Prosecutors keen to nail the men who were once pitted against the West German authorities during the Cold War argued that while the men's actions took place in former East Germany they had their effect in West Germany.
